newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA MAY CLOSE MORE BANKS - C.BANK GOVERNOR.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA MAY CLOSE MORE BANKS - C.BANK GOVERNOR.

text.p: The Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) will possibly seek the closure of more local banks as part of a long-delayed financial stablisation programme, BNB governor Lyubomir Filipov told Reuter Financial Television.
Asked in a telephone interview with RFTV about further bank closures, Filipov said,"It is possible. We are facing a further restructuring which may include possible closures of banks."
He said the socialist government would announce "in two to five days a very large programme of fast privatisation" in a bid to raise desperately needed cash for debt payments.
"There is a shortlist. The (BNB) board is dicussing the possible banks which are going to be asked for closure," said Filipov, who stepped out of a board meeting for the interview.
Monday's newspapers had carried an unofficial list of up to 14 banks likely to be closed or merged amid speculation of an imminent announcement.
Filipov urged foreign investors to buy the state companies that the government plans to offer in the near future.

"Foreign investors are invited to buy enterprises in this country. (Then) the foreign exchange reserves will increase and the BNB will be in a position to help those banks that remain in the system after this possible restructuring is completed," he said.

Earlier on Thursday the Bank Consolidation Company, which manages state equity in commercial banks, said the government planned to privatise seven of the country's eight state-owned banks, leaving only Bulbank untouched.
The sell-off plans include Balkanbank and Economic Bank, which feature on the list circulated in the local media.
The other five banks expected to be sold are Biohim Bank, Bulgarian Post Bank, Hebros Bank, Express Bank and United Bulgarian Bank.

The government, battling an economic crisis, is under pressure from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to speed up structural reforms in the banking sector as a crucial element of a funding programme agreed in July.
The IMF postponed a second $115 million tranche this month due to Bulgaria's failure to close down scores of loss-making state firms and several insolvent banks.

Filipov said he was optimistic about Bulgaria winning the second tranche of funding from the IMF. However he added: "I am half-optimistic to what extent these measures will help a total improvement of the financial situation in the country."
"We have to do a lot to attract foreign exchange from all possible sources," he said.
The Bulgarian Telecommunications Company and a chemical giant Sodi Devnya are among the enterprises due to be offered for sale shortly. -- Elisaveta Konstantinova, Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-84561
